title: Der Schlüssel im Wagen  (The Key in the Trolley)

segments.t: Out in the supermarket aisles, a friendly shopper flags Pina down with an everyday German shopping mishap: he used his house key to unlock a trolley, and now the key refuses to come back out. Pina points him toward veteran colleague Wilhelm and offers to grab a proper plastic token. Listen to the German conversation first.
Hallo! Ich habe hier ein Problem mit dem Wagen.
Mein Schlüssel geht da leider nicht mehr raus.
Frag mal nach Wilhelm, ich glaube, das kommt öfter vor.
Er kennt sich damit gut aus.
Ich weiß jetzt nicht, was ich da machen soll.
Es wäre ja schade wegen des Schlüssels.
Danke, das ist sehr lieb von dir!
Gerne! Ich hole dir noch schnell einen Chip.
Danke schön!
Let's walk through how the customer explains his stuck key and how Pina points him to the right person.
Hallo! Ich habe hier ein Problem mit dem Wagen.

'Hello! I have a problem with the trolley here.' Saying 'I have a problem with...' works almost word for word like English. Notice that the everyday word for 'car' or 'wagon' is also what shoppers call a supermarket trolley.
Mein Schlüssel geht da leider nicht mehr raus.

'Unfortunately my key will not come out of there anymore.' Where English says a key 'won't come out', German literally says it 'goes not more out', pairing 'not anymore' right before the directional word 'out'.
Frag mal nach Wilhelm, ich glaube, das kommt öfter vor.

'Ask for Wilhelm — I think that happens pretty often.' Asking for a person uses the preposition for 'after' — literally 'ask once after Wilhelm'. Then 'comes more often forward' is the natural German idiom for something happening fairly often.
Er kennt sich damit gut aus.

'He really knows his way around that.' This handy expression builds on 'know' plus 'oneself' and 'out' at the end: whenever someone knows a topic, machine, or neighbourhood inside out, this is the phrase to reach for.
Ich weiß jetzt nicht, was ich da machen soll.

'I don't really know right now what I should do with it.' Notice Pina uses the word for knowing a fact rather than the word for knowing people that Titus used earlier, because she's talking about knowing what step to take.
Danke, das ist sehr lieb von dir!

'Thanks, that is very sweet of you!' Calling something 'sweet' or 'dear of you' sounds warm and appreciative among younger speakers, especially since the two of them immediately use the informal 'you'.
Gerne! Ich hole dir noch schnell einen Chip.

'Gladly! I'll quickly grab a trolley token for you too.' That single word for 'gladly' is the friendliest everyday answer to 'thank you' in Germany — light, upbeat, and reusable in every shop or cafe. Now let's hear the whole aisle conversation again.
Hallo! Ich habe hier ein Problem mit dem Wagen.
Mein Schlüssel geht da leider nicht mehr raus.
Frag mal nach Wilhelm, ich glaube, das kommt öfter vor.
Er kennt sich damit gut aus.
Ich weiß jetzt nicht, was ich da machen soll.
Es wäre ja schade wegen des Schlüssels.
Danke, das ist sehr lieb von dir!
Gerne! Ich hole dir noch schnell einen Chip.
Danke schön!

Armed with Pina's tip to find Wilhelm, the grateful customer heads off to rescue his house key. You now have natural phrases for explaining a problem with something, saying an item won't come out, saying someone knows their stuff, and thanking someone warmly. See you next time!
Bis später!
